slides.title: Storage and delay errors
bullets: Collected urine should be tested within one hour.
If the test is delayed, bacteria multiply and use up glucose: the glucose result is wrong, the pH shifts to alkaline, red cells lyse and casts break down.
Until testing begins, specimens are kept in a refrigerator.
Appearance and colour are judged in the light and recorded; turbidity may come from many epithelial cells in a badly collected sample, red cells, white cells, bacteria or salts.

slides.title: False results
bullets: Protein: false positives if disinfectants or vaginal or urethral discharge get into the sample, or if the urine is very alkaline.
Glucose: ascorbic acid and some drugs and high catalase activity give false negatives; residues of disinfectants such as bleaching powder give false positives.

Bilirubin: protect fresh urine from sunlight and fluorescent light — bilirubin oxidises quickly to biliverdin, for which the strip has no reagent; nitrites reduce sensitivity; phenazopyridine may give a false positive.
Positive results are pathological; if protein is found the urine is also examined microscopically.

slides.title: False results
bullets: If sugar is found in the urine of a patient not known to have diabetes, the blood is also tested.

slides.title: Sources of error and interpretation
bullets: If urine stands for more than an hour after collection, red cells lyse and casts break down.
Kurbonova: normally up to 5–6 white cells and 0–2 red cells per field, no casts; Aripova writes that red cells are not normally present (except in samples taken during menstruation).
Dirt on cover glasses and slides and foreign objects from the air (wool, pollen, cotton fibres) may be mistaken for sediment elements.

In the Nechiporenko method the formed elements in 1 mL of urine are counted in a Goryaev chamber; calculation formulas and reference values differ between the sources, so follow the laboratory’s instructions.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: An unsuitable specimen (after an enema, laxative or oil, colouring drugs, mixed with urine) spoils the result.
If the preparation regimen (food of a set composition) was not followed, linking the food remains found to a digestive disorder is unreliable.
Neutral fat and fatty acids cannot be told apart by appearance alone: methylene blue stains only fatty-acid drops.
Iodine breaks down when Lugol’s solution is stored for long — make it fresh every month.
Some findings have no diagnostic value (for example cholesterol crystals, bits of cartilage and bone) — do not read them as a sign of disease.

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Non-parasitic structures may be mistaken for parasites: vegetable and muscle fibres, pollen, starch cells, fat particles, yeasts, spores, soaps, hairs, fatty-acid crystals and air bubbles.
Laxatives, antacids, contrast media and some antibiotics may interfere with finding parasites.
If the slide dries or the specimen is late, motile trophozoites are not found; a parasite shed intermittently may be missed in a single specimen.
With too much light colourless eggs cannot be seen — close the condenser.

slides.title: Sources of error and quality control
bullets: Quality depends on standardised methods and the skill of the staff: the laboratory should have positive slides or pictures against which the parasites found are compared.
